s001.heard: Two people borrow money to make something grow. Salim makes shoes. He borrows to fill a big order. He delivers it, makes a good profit, and repays the loan.

s002.heard: Swapna is a small farmer. She borrows to grow groundnut. The crop fails, and she has to sell part of her land. Same tool, opposite results. So what decides whether credit helps or traps?

s003.heard: In part one we saw what money is. In part two, how banks create it. Now we ask who gets it, at what price, and how it moves from one hand to another.

s004.heard: We take it in four steps. What credit is, and what it costs. Who lends, banks or moneylenders. Groups that help the poor borrow. And how payments move, from a cheque to a phone tap. We end with a Prelims question from 2024. This is part three of three.

s005.heard: NCERT defines credit, or a loan, as an agreement. The lender supplies money, goods or services. The borrower promises to pay later. Every loan has terms of credit. The interest rate. The documents needed. The mode of repayment. And collateral. An asset the borrower owns, which the lender may sell if the loan is not repaid.

s006.heard: Now go back to Swapna. Repaying her loan depended crucially on income from her farm. When the crop failed, she could not repay, and the debt grew. NCERT calls this a debt trap. Credit pushed her into a situation from which recovery is very painful. NCERT says whether credit helps depends on the risks, and on whether there is some support in case of loss.

s007.heard: Where do people borrow? NCERT sorts lenders into two kinds. Formal lenders are banks and cooperatives. Informal lenders include moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends.

s008.heard: A government survey, the NSO's seventy-seventh round, counted debt on the thirtieth of June 2018. It says institutional and non-institutional. In rural India, institutional, or formal, lenders held sixty-six percent of outstanding cash debt, and others thirty-four. In urban India, eighty-seven and thirteen.

s009.heard: Here is an exam trap. NCERT's text says formal lenders meet only about half of rural credit needs. But NCERT's own graph shows formal lenders at sixty-six percent. Both are in NCERT. The graph matches the survey, so use the graph, and name the survey.

s010.heard: Formal and informal lenders also differ in who watches them. NCERT says the Reserve Bank supervises formal lenders. It checks that banks keep the minimum cash balance. Banks report how much they lend, to whom, and at what interest rate. NCERT adds that no organisation supervises informal lenders.

s011.heard: NCERT's summary says richer households receive formal credit, while the poor depend on informal sources. The poor should get a much greater share. Why is that hard? NCERT says absence of collateral is one of the major reasons the poor cannot get bank loans. Its next example shows one way around it.

s012.heard: A typical self-help group has fifteen to twenty members. Each saves a small amount regularly, from twenty-five rupees to a hundred or more. After a year or two of regular saving, the group becomes eligible for a bank loan in the group's name. NCERT says banks lend to such groups even without collateral, because the group is responsible for repayment.

s013.heard: On the thirty-first of March 2024, NABARD counted about one hundred and forty-four lakh groups with savings linked to banks. About seventy-seven lakh were also linked to bank credit.

s014.heard: NCERT's other example is Grameen Bank of Bangladesh. In 2006, the Norwegian Nobel Committee honoured Muhammad Yunus and Grameen Bank. It honoured their efforts to create economic and social development from below. In 2006, the Committee's chairman said over ninety-five percent of Grameen Bank's borrowers are women.

s015.heard: Access also starts with an account. The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana had fifty-nine point oh nine crore accounts on the nineteenth of August 2026. Women are fifty-five point seven percent of the account holders. And seventy-seven point eight percent of the accounts were in rural and semi-urban areas. Those are the Finance Ministry's figures, released on the twenty-seventh of August 2026.

s016.heard: Other institutions help too. Post offices run savings schemes, such as National Savings Certificates and Kisan Vikas Patra. NABARD funds banks that lend for farming, village industries and rural infrastructure. And the Reserve Bank is the banker to banks.

s017.heard: NCERT lists three kinds of bank account. A savings account pays interest, with limited withdrawals. A current account is for businesses, and pays no interest. A fixed deposit holds your money for a fixed period, usually at higher interest.

s018.heard: NCERT's compounding example, one thousand rupees at six percent a year grows for twelve years. It becomes two thousand and twelve rupees and twenty paise.

s019.heard: Now, how money moves. To get cash, you use a withdrawal slip, or an ATM with a debit card and a PIN. To move money between accounts, you can write a cheque. It is paper, and it takes time. Or you pay electronically, a debit card at a shop machine, net banking, or a mobile payment.

s020.heard: NCERT describes UPI, the Unified Payments Interface. The National Payments Corporation of India, NPCI, launched it in 2016. It moves money between bank accounts using a QR code or a phone number. The steps, the payer's app, the payer's bank, then NPCI, which checks the UPI PIN and processes the payment. Last comes the receiver's bank.

s021.heard: How big is it? In June 2026, the Reserve Bank's provisional data show UPI handled about two thousand, two hundred and seventy-two crore payments. The average payment was about one thousand, two hundred and seventy-three rupees.

s022.heard: In the same month, UPI payments outnumbered cheques about five hundred and thirty-four to one. The cheques are those cleared through the Cheque Truncation System. RTGS handled about three point two crore payments, and the average was about seventy-two lakh rupees.

s023.heard: NCERT warns that digital payments have made life easier, but users must beware of fraud. NCERT's advice, never share account numbers, passwords or OTPs with strangers, and avoid clicking unknown links. In case of fraud, call the helpline one nine three zero, or use the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal.

s024.heard: Now a Prelims question. In 2024, UPSC asked about syndicated loans. Statement one, syndicated lending spreads the risk of a borrower's default across several lenders. Statement two, a syndicated loan can be a fixed lump sum, but cannot be a credit line.

s025.heard: A 2004 BIS article says the syndicated loan market allows a more efficient geographical and institutional sharing of risk. A March 2022 Bank for International Settlements article says a group of lenders grants a syndicated loan to one borrower. Each funds part of it. The same article shows syndicated loans come as both credit lines and term loans. So, by our reasoning, statement one is correct and statement two is not. That points to option C. We did not read UPSC's own answer key.

s026.heard: For the exam, write it this way. Credit is an agreement. The lender supplies money, and the borrower promises to pay later. Terms of credit are the interest rate, collateral, documents and mode of repayment. Whether credit helps depends on the risk, and on support if things go wrong. The Reserve Bank supervises formal lenders. No organisation supervises informal lenders. Self-help groups let the poor borrow in the group's name. UPI moves money between bank accounts through NPCI

s027.heard: So, in three parts. On NCERT's account, money is cash and deposits. A loan opens a new deposit, within limits. And credit can help or trap. Salim and Swapna both borrowed. NCERT says what matters is the risk, and whether there is support if things go wrong.
